name: Algebraic Expressions
what_is_it: An algebraic expression uses letters (variables) to represent unknown or changing numbers, combined with numbers and operations. Grade 8 focuses on simplifying expressions by collecting like terms, and substitution (replacing letters with given numbers).
why_it_matters: Algebra generalises arithmetic — instead of solving one specific number problem, an expression describes a whole family of situations at once. It's the language used in nearly every other maths and science topic from here on.
key_vocabulary: Variable — a letter representing an unknown or changing value, e.g. x
Coefficient — the number multiplying a variable, e.g. 5 in 5x
Term — a single part of an expression separated by + or −, e.g. 3x, −2y, 7
Like terms — terms with exactly the same variable(s) and exponent, e.g. 3x and −5x
Constant — a term with no variable, just a number
core_concept: Only LIKE terms can be added or subtracted together. Simplifying means collecting like terms into a single term. Substitution means replacing each variable with a given numeric value and then calculating.
rules: Only combine terms with identical variables and identical exponents.
Keep the sign attached to each term when rearranging.
Multiply coefficients and add exponents of the same base when multiplying terms: 2x × 3x = 6x².
When substituting negative numbers, always use brackets to avoid sign errors.
formulae: Distributive law: a(b + c) = ab + ac
step_by_step_method: STEP 1: Identify all the terms in the expression.
STEP 2: Group terms that have exactly the same variable and exponent.
STEP 3: Add/subtract the coefficients of each like-term group.
STEP 4: Write the simplified expression, usually from highest to lowest power.
STEP 5 (substitution): Replace each variable with its given value in brackets, then calculate using BODMAS.
fast_method: Underline or colour-code each family of like terms before combining — this stops you from accidentally mixing x-terms with x²-terms or y-terms.
why_fast_method_works: Like terms represent the same 'kind' of quantity (just like you can't add 3 apples and 2 oranges to get 5 apple-oranges) — visually grouping them prevents combining unrelated quantities.
common_mistakes: Adding x and x² together as if they were like terms.
Forgetting brackets when substituting negative numbers, causing sign errors.
Dropping a negative sign when rearranging terms.
Multiplying coefficients incorrectly when the expression has more than two terms.
memory_trick: "Same letter, same power, same family — only family members can be added together."
visual_explanation: Colour-grouping diagram: all x-terms in blue, all y-terms in green, constants in grey, so learners can visually collect each colour group.
guided_example:
Simplify: 5a − 3b + 2a + b − 4
1) Group a-terms: 5a + 2a = 7a
2) Group b-terms: −3b + b = −2b
3) Constant: −4
Answer: 7a − 2b − 4
challenge_question: Simplify fully: 3(2x + 5) − 2(x − 4), then evaluate the result when x = 3.
mastery_check: Mastered when a student reliably identifies like terms in mixed expressions, simplifies without sign errors, and substitutes negative values correctly using brackets.
